source.carries_no_document: Opened and read in full 2026-08-11 (https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chicago_River&action=raw, HTTP 200). Looked for a transcription of Swearingen's 1803 journal and there is none: the page paraphrases him in one sentence of its own prose and footnotes the reprinting, which is a citation and not a reprinting. Every other passage this project draws on here is the same shape. So this record's rung is a judgement about an encyclopedia article — later scholarship, tier 4 — and the documents behind it have to be fetched on their own terms. Where it sends you: Quaife 1913, pp. 373-377 for Swearingen; Holland, Chicago in Maps (2005), pp. 102-109 and Andreas vol. 1, pp. 234-235 for the harbour works.
source.citation: "Chicago River." Wikipedia. Paraphrasing Lt. James Strode Swearingen's 1803 description of the river at Fort Dearborn, footnoted to its reprinting in Quaife 1913, and the 1833-37 harbour works after Holland and Andreas.
what_it_does_not_supply: channel width or depth at the forks

one word of Swearingen's journal — the page paraphrases and footnotes it; the reprinting it names (Quaife 1913, pp. 373-377) was opened 2026-08-11 and is quaife_1913_swearingen, which supersedes this record on every 1803 river figure
the north bank's height: its '6 ft' is arithmetic on a bounded visual estimate and appears nowhere in the journal
the two sentences that matter most to this project — the river standing dead behind a sand-stopped mouth, and the banks above being quite low — both of which the paraphrase drops
any sourced statement of the river's surface gradient: the sluggish-flow sentence the flat water surface rests on carries no footnote of its own
what_it_supplies: a finding aid to the 1833-1837 harbour works chronology, after Holland and Andreas
the footnote that located the primary printing of Swearingen — its most valuable contribution to this project, now discharged into quaife_1913_swearingen
